issues.legal_issue: A gift deed procured by fraud about its contents is voidable, and limitation for setting it aside begins when the fraud becomes known.
material_facts: The donor was young, illiterate, and dependent on her husband, who managed her affairs and could dominate her will.
She believed the deed concerned only property associated with her husband, but it also included valuable property she had inherited from her father, without her knowledge.
She discovered the inclusion after her husband's death and filed suit within a few days of learning of the fraud.
issues.conclusion: The misrepresentation concerned the contents, not the character, of the deed, so the transaction was voidable rather than void. The claim was governed by Article 95 of the Limitation Act, 1908, and was timely because it was filed shortly after the fraud became known. The deed was not binding as to the fraudulently included property, and the donor was entitled to recover possession of it.
issues.legal_principle: A transaction induced by fraud is generally voidable, not void; fraudulent misrepresentation about a document's contents differs from misrepresentation about its character, which may make the transaction void. Under Article 95 of the Limitation Act, 1908, limitation runs from when the fraud becomes known to the party wronged. The Court referred to Clough v. L. & N. W. Railway, Foster v. Mackinon, Sanni Bibi v. Siddik Hossain, and Brindaban v. Dhurba Charan.

rule.if: instrument_cancellation_suit and fraud_concerned_document_contents and fraud_discovered_after_execution and suit_filed_within_limitation_after_discovery

predicates.instrument_cancellation_suit: The claimant brought a suit to set aside an instrument.
predicates.fraud_concerned_document_contents: The other party fraudulently included property in the instrument without the claimant's knowledge, while the claimant understood the instrument to concern different property.
predicates.fraud_discovered_after_execution: The claimant learned of the fraudulent inclusion after the instrument was executed.
predicates.suit_filed_within_limitation_after_disco: The claimant filed suit within the applicable limitation period after discovering the fraud.

issues.definition: When an instrument-cancellation suit concerns a fraudulent inclusion that the claimant discovered only after execution, a suit filed within the limitation period after that discovery makes the fraud-based claim timely.

issues.legal_issue: For a suit to set aside an instrument for undue influence, limitation begins when the claimant knows the facts entitling them to set it aside, not when the influence ends.
material_facts: The donor's husband was in a position of active confidence and could dominate her will when she made the gift.
The gift appeared unconscionable, and the evidence did not rebut the presumption that it was induced by undue influence.
The donor knew when she executed the deed that her husband had prevailed upon her to convey the relevant property through undue influence.
She brought suit after the limitation period had run from that knowledge, although she argued that the period should run only after she escaped her husband's influence.
issues.conclusion: The claim was governed by Article 91 of the Limitation Act, 1908, and was time-barred because the donor knew the facts entitling her to set aside the deed when she executed it. Continued subjection to the husband's influence did not postpone the start of limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(3) of the Indian Contract Act places the burden of proving that a transaction was not induced by undue influence on the person able to dominate another's will when the transaction appears unconscionable. Section 111 of the Indian Evidence Act places the burden of proving good faith on a person in a position of active confidence. Under Article 91 of the Limitation Act, 1908, limitation for setting aside an instrument begins when the claimant knows the facts entitling them to that relief, not when they escape the influence. The Court applied Someshwar Dutt v. Tirbhawan Dutt.

rule.if: instrument_cancellation_suit and undue_influence_induced_transaction and claimant_knew_grounds_at_execution and suit_filed_after_limitation_from_knowledge

predicates.instrument_cancellation_suit: The claimant brought a suit to set aside an instrument.
predicates.undue_influence_induced_transaction: A person able to dominate the claimant's will procured a transaction that appeared unconscionable, and the evidence did not rebut that it was induced by undue influence.
predicates.claimant_knew_grounds_at_execution: The claimant knew, when executing the instrument, the facts that entitled them to seek its cancellation for undue influence.
predicates.suit_filed_after_limitation_from_knowled: The claimant filed suit after the applicable limitation period had run from learning those facts.

issues.definition: When an instrument-cancellation suit concerns a transaction induced by undue influence, knowledge of the grounds at execution and filing after the applicable period from that knowledge make the claim time-barred.
